content: A medical ventilator is an automated device designed to mechanically deliver breathable air into and out of the lungs. It is used to provide respiratory support for patients who are either unable to breathe on their own or are breathing inadequately. Ventilators are primarily utilized in intensive care units, home care settings, emergency medicine (as standalone units), and as part of anesthesia machines during surgical procedures. Modern positive pressure ventilators consist of several key components: a compressible air reservoir, air and oxygen supplies, a system of valves and tubes, and a patient circuit that can be disposable or reusable. The air reservoir is pneumatically compressed multiple times per minute to deliver either room air or, more commonly, a mixture of air and oxygen to the patient. When the pressure is released, the patient exhales passively due to the natural elasticity of the lungs. The exhaled air is typically expelled through a one-way valve within the patient circuit. The oxygen concentration of the inspired gas can be adjusted from 21% (ambient air) to 100% (pure oxygen). Pressure and flow characteristics can be set either mechanically or electronically, depending on the ventilator's design. Modern ventilators are often controlled by computer systems, which allow precise adjustments to pressure and flow settings tailored to the individual needs of the patient. These fine-tuned settings not only optimize ventilation but also enhance patient comfort and tolerance. In countries like Germany, Canada, and the United States, respiratory therapists are responsible for adjusting these settings based on parameters such as inhaled air, patient pressure, and exhaled air. Depending on the type of ventilation required, the patient interface may be noninvasive (e.g., a nasal mask) or invasive (e.g., intubation). For long-term ventilator dependence, a tracheostomy is typically preferred over laryngeal or nasal intubation, as it is more comfortable and practical for extended care. Mechanical ventilators are classified as life-critical systems because their failure can result in death. As such, they are designed with high reliability and redundancy to prevent single points of failure. Most ventilators include manual backup mechanisms for hand-driven respiration in the event of power loss. Additionally, some systems are equipped with compressed gas tanks, backup batteries, and fail-safe mechanisms to ensure continued operation during power outages or equipment malfunctions. These systems may also include methods to alert caregivers or call for assistance if the ventilator's mechanisms or software fail. The history of mechanical ventilation dates back to the development of the iron lung, a noninvasive negative pressure ventilator widely used during the polio epidemics of the 20th century. The first widely recognized version, the Drinker respirator, was introduced in 1928, with subsequent improvements made by John Haven Emerson in 1931. Other noninvasive ventilators used for polio patients included biphasic cuirass ventilation, the rocking bed, and early positive pressure machines. In 1949, Emerson collaborated with Harvard University’s anesthesia department to develop a mechanical ventilator for anesthesia. By the 1950s, mechanical ventilators became increasingly common in anesthesia and intensive care, driven by the need to treat polio patients and the growing use of muscle relaxants during surgery. These relaxants, while improving surgical conditions, paralyze respiratory muscles, necessitating mechanical ventilation. In the United States, the Bird ventilator was an early gas-driven model that required no electrical power. In the United Kingdom, the East Radcliffe and Beaver models were early examples, with the latter using an automotive wiper motor to drive the bellows. However, electric motors posed a hazard in operating theaters due to the risk of explosions in the presence of flammable anesthetics like ether and cyclopropane. In 1952, Roger Manley of Westminster Hospital in London developed a gas-driven ventilator that became the most popular model in Europe. This design was independent of electrical power and posed no explosion risk. The Manley Mark II, developed in collaboration with the Blease company, became a robust and widely used unit. Its operation relied on a simple mechanism where incoming gas flow lifted a weighted bellows, which then fell under gravity to deliver breathing gases to the patient. The inflation pressure and gas volume could be adjusted using movable weights and sliders, respectively. This design facilitated the adoption of positive pressure ventilation techniques in mainstream European anesthetic practice. High-frequency percussive ventilation (HFPV) emerged in the 1980s as a hybrid of conventional mechanical ventilation and high-frequency oscillatory ventilation. It has been used to manage patients with persistent hypoxemia unresponsive to conventional ventilation and, in some cases, as a primary mode of ventilatory support from the outset.
